nodes.title: REST APIs: Key Ideas
nodes.content: REST is the dominant style for web APIs: resources addressed by URLs, manipulated with HTTP methods, returning structured data (usually JSON). Network-automation and developer certs (DevNet, ServiceNow) assume you can read and call one.

flashcards.front: How do HTTP methods map to operations?
flashcards.back: GET reads a resource (safe, no side effects), POST creates, PUT/PATCH update (replace vs partial), DELETE removes. Combined with a resource URL (e.g. /api/v1/devices/42) they express CRUD over HTTP.

flashcards.front: What do common HTTP status codes mean?
flashcards.back: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content); 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 rate-limited); 5xx server error. The class tells you whether to fix the request or retry.

flashcards.front: How is a REST call usually authenticated?
flashcards.back: Via an HTTP header — a bearer token (OAuth 2.0 'Authorization: Bearer ...'), an API key, or basic auth. Tokens are obtained first (e.g. an OAuth token endpoint) and sent on each subsequent request.

Idempotent methods (GET, PUT, DELETE) produce the same result if repeated — safe to retry; POST usually isn't. Large result sets are paginated (limit/offset or cursor/next-link) so clients fetch pages rather than everything at once.

questions.q: A developer issues a POST to `/api/v1/devices` and the server creates the new device record. According to REST conventions, which HTTP status code should the API return, and what header is typically included?
choices: 200 OK with a `Content-Length` header pointing at the new resource
201 Created with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource URI
202 Accepted with a `Retry-After` header for polling
204 No Content with an empty response body and no headers
questions.explanation: When a POST successfully creates a resource the standard response is 201 Created together with a `Location` header that contains the URI of the newly-created resource. 200 OK is used for successful GET/PUT that returns a body, 202 Accepted means the request was queued for asynchronous processing, and 204 No Content means success with deliberately no body (typical for DELETE).

questions.q: You are integrating a third-party application with the Webex REST API on behalf of end users. The application must let each user grant scoped, revocable access without exposing their Webex password. Which authentication mechanism is the correct fit?
choices: HTTP Basic authentication with the user's Webex email and password
A long-lived static API key embedded in the application binary
Mutual TLS using the application's X.509 client certificate
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code grant returning a short-lived access token
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 with the Authorization Code grant is designed exactly for this: the user authenticates directly with Webex, consents to specific scopes, and the app receives a short-lived access token (plus refresh token) without ever seeing the password. Basic auth exposes credentials, a static embedded key is not per-user and cannot be revoked granularly, and mTLS authenticates the app itself rather than a delegated user.

questions.q: A network engineer wants to programmatically configure an IOS XE device using a YANG-defined data model over a session-oriented, transactional protocol that supports candidate configurations and `commit`/`rollback`. Which protocol meets these requirements?
choices: NETCONF over SSH on TCP/830
RESTCONF over HTTPS on TCP/443
gNMI over HTTP/2 on TCP/9339
SNMPv3 over UDP/161 with SET PDUs
questions.explanation: NETCONF runs over SSH on TCP/830, maintains a persistent session, and supports the `<candidate>` datastore with `<commit>` and `<discard-changes>`/rollback — true transactional configuration. RESTCONF is stateless HTTP and exposes YANG data per-request without a candidate-store transaction. gNMI is Google's streaming-telemetry/configuration protocol but does not use the NETCONF candidate/commit model. SNMP has no YANG or transactional semantics.

questions.q: Two developers have been working on parallel feature branches. Before merging into `main`, the team lead wants the feature history to appear as a single linear sequence of commits on top of the latest `main` — without any merge-commit bubbles. Which Git operation should each developer run on their feature branch first?
choices: `git merge main` to fast-forward main into the feature branch
`git cherry-pick main` to copy main's commits onto the feature branch
`git rebase main` to replay the feature commits on top of main
`git reset --hard main` to align the branch with main
questions.explanation: `git rebase main` rewrites the feature branch so its commits are replayed on top of the current `main`, producing a linear history with no merge commits when the branch is finally fast-forwarded in. `git merge main` would create exactly the merge-commit bubble the lead wants to avoid. `git cherry-pick` copies individual commits, not a branch, and is the wrong tool here. `git reset --hard main` would destroy the feature work entirely.

nodes.title: Cisco platform automation (DevNet): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Cisco exposes programmable REST APIs across its platforms — Webex, Meraki Dashboard, and Catalyst Center (DNA Center) — so you can automate collaboration and network operations. The DevNet Associate exam tests how you authenticate, page through results, and react to events via webhooks.

flashcards.front: How do you typically authenticate to Cisco platform REST APIs like Meraki and Webex?
flashcards.back: With a bearer token sent in the HTTP Authorization header — Meraki uses an API key, Webex uses an OAuth/bot access token. Catalyst Center issues a short-lived token from its authentication endpoint that you then send on each request.

flashcards.front: What is the Meraki Dashboard API used for?
flashcards.back: Programmatic management of Meraki organizations, networks, and devices over REST — provisioning, configuration, and pulling telemetry from the cloud-managed Dashboard instead of clicking the UI.

flashcards.front: Why and how do these APIs use pagination?
flashcards.back: To return large result sets in chunks. Clients follow paging controls (e.g., page-size limits plus Link/next-page references or query parameters) to retrieve every record instead of one huge response.

flashcards.front: What is a webhook and how does it differ from polling?
flashcards.back: A webhook is a server-to-client HTTP callback: the platform POSTs an event (e.g., a Webex message or Meraki alert) to your URL when it happens, so you react in real time instead of repeatedly polling the API for changes.

questions.q: A script that pulls clients from the Meraki Dashboard API receives an HTTP 200 with a `Link` header containing `rel="next"`. What does this indicate and what should the script do?
choices: The API is rate-limited; the script must back off using the Retry-After value
The response is paginated; the script should follow the `next` URL to retrieve the remaining records
The organization has been migrated; the script should re-authenticate against the new region
A schema change has occurred; the script should fetch the OpenAPI spec from the `next` link
questions.explanation: The Meraki Dashboard API paginates large result sets and returns RFC 5988 `Link` headers with `rel="first"`, `rel="prev"`, `rel="next"`, `rel="last"`. A `rel="next"` link means more pages exist and the client should issue a GET against that URL to continue. Rate-limit signalling uses 429 with `Retry-After`, region migrations are signalled with 3xx redirects to a regional base URL, and schema discovery is unrelated to pagination headers.

questions.q: Your team needs a single controller that provides intent-based, automated provisioning, assurance and segmentation for an enterprise **campus and branch LAN/Wi-Fi** fabric. Which Cisco platform is purpose-built for this scope?
choices: Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center)
Cisco vManage (Catalyst SD-WAN Manager)
Cisco APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller)
Cisco Intersight
questions.explanation: Cisco DNA Center / Catalyst Center is the intent-based controller for enterprise campus and branch LAN/Wi-Fi (SD-Access fabric, assurance, automated provisioning). vManage is the controller for SD-WAN (WAN overlays between sites), not LAN/Wi-Fi. APIC is the controller for the ACI data-center fabric. Intersight is for compute/UCS and HyperFlex infrastructure lifecycle.

questions.q: A developer runs `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` followed by `docker run -d myapp:1.0`. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship between the two artifacts produced?
choices: The image is a running instance; the container is the immutable read-only template
Image and container are interchangeable terms; Docker uses them as synonyms
The container is the build cache; the image is the running process namespace
The image is an immutable, layered read-only template; the container is a running, writable instance of that image
questions.explanation: A Docker image is built once from a Dockerfile and is an immutable, layered, read-only template. `docker run` instantiates a container from that image by adding a thin writable layer on top and starting the entry-point process inside isolated namespaces. The other options invert or conflate the two concepts.

questions.q: An app currently polls a Webex REST endpoint every 5 seconds to learn when new messages are posted in a room. Traffic and quota usage are excessive. Which mechanism would let Webex notify the app only when a relevant event actually occurs?
choices: Increase the polling interval to 60 seconds and add exponential backoff
Register a Webex webhook with a public HTTPS callback URL filtered by room and resource
Open an SSH tunnel to the Webex API and read events from its standard output
Use SNMP traps from the Webex cloud to the application
questions.explanation: Webhooks invert the polling pattern: the app registers an HTTPS callback URL plus a resource/event filter (e.g. `messages`/`created` for a specific room), and Webex POSTs an event payload to that URL only when the event fires — eliminating most quota usage. Slower polling is still polling. SSH tunnelling is not a Webex API pattern, and SNMP is a network-management protocol unrelated to Webex collaboration APIs.

nodes.title: Automation and IaC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

questions.q: While reviewing a containerised microservice against the Twelve-Factor App methodology, you notice the database password is hard-coded into a `config.py` file checked into Git. Which factor does this violate, and what is the recommended remediation?
choices: Factor I (Codebase) — split the repository into one repo per environment
Factor VI (Processes) — make the process stateful so credentials persist in memory
Factor III (Config) — store config (including secrets) in environment variables, not in code
Factor X (Dev/prod parity) — ensure prod and dev share the same hard-coded credentials
questions.explanation: Twelve-Factor Factor III, Config, says strict separation of config from code: anything that varies between deploys (credentials, host names, endpoints) belongs in environment variables, not in source. Factor I argues for one codebase tracked in revision control with many deploys (not per-env repos). Factor VI explicitly requires processes to be stateless. Factor X is about keeping environments as similar as possible — never by sharing the same hard-coded secret.

questions.q: An Ansible playbook with the task `ios_config: lines: ['ntp server 10.0.0.1']` is run twice against the same router. After the second run the change report shows `changed=0`. Which Ansible property explains this behaviour?
choices: Eventual consistency — Ansible needs a third run to converge
Push-mode delivery — the second run was silently dropped by the SSH transport
Stateless execution — Ansible always reports `changed=0` after the first run
Idempotency — modules check current state and only apply changes when actual state differs from declared state
questions.explanation: Ansible modules are designed to be idempotent: `ios_config` reads the running configuration, compares it against the declared `lines`, and only pushes a change if the line is missing. Re-running a converged playbook therefore reports `changed=0`. The other options describe behaviours that Ansible does not have: there is no eventual-consistency lag, runs are not silently dropped, and `changed=0` is the result of a state check, not a stateless default.

questions.q: You are building a Webex chatbot that must reply in any space it is added to. Which credential should the bot use to authenticate to the Webex REST API, and what is its key security property?
choices: A Bot access token issued when the bot is created on developer.webex.com — it is scoped to the bot account and only sees messages addressed to it in group spaces
The developer's personal access token — it inherits the developer's full user permissions and never expires
A guest-issuer JWT signed with the organisation's shared secret — it grants admin-equivalent access to every space
An OAuth client secret used directly as a bearer token in the Authorization header
questions.explanation: Bots authenticate with a dedicated Bot access token generated when the bot is registered on developer.webex.com. It identifies the bot as its own user, and in group spaces the bot only receives messages where it is explicitly @-mentioned — an important privacy property. A personal access token is for development only and tied to a human identity. Guest-issuer tokens are for embedding guest users (not bots) and are not admin-level. OAuth client secrets are used to *obtain* tokens, not as bearer tokens themselves.

questions.q: In a Cisco ACI fabric, which controller exposes the northbound REST API that developers use to define tenants, application profiles, EPGs and contracts as JSON or XML objects in the Management Information Tree?
choices: Cisco DNA Center (Catalyst Center)
Cisco vManage (Catalyst SD-WAN Manager)
Cisco APIC (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller)
Cisco Intersight
questions.explanation: APIC is the centralised policy controller for an ACI data-center fabric and exposes the REST API used to read and write objects in the Management Information Tree (MIT) — tenants, application profiles, EPGs, contracts, bridge domains, etc. DNA Center / Catalyst Center is the controller for campus/branch SD-Access, vManage is the controller for SD-WAN, and Intersight manages UCS/HyperFlex compute infrastructure.
